cards.prompt: After "Ready, set," a model gives "go" a 70% chance at temperature 1. At which temperature is it **most likely** to pick "go"?

options.text: It's the same at every temperature

cards.explanation: A **low** temperature makes the top token even likelier: at 0.2, "go" has over 99%. At 2, the chances even out and "go" drops below 50%.

cards.prompt: A model gives the next word a **30%** chance. If it carries on from the same text **300** times, about how many times will it pick that word?
Which word is this model **most likely** to pick next?
cards.explanation: "Raining cats and **dogs**" is a common saying, so it's by far the most likely next word, even though it isn't what rain is made of. The model picks what usually comes next.

cards.prompt: Would each job be better with a **low** temperature, or a **higher** one?

items.label: Writing code that has to work

cards.explanation: Code and facts have one right answer: **low**. Names and jokes want variety: **higher**.

cards.prompt: Why can a chatbot confidently name a book that doesn't exist?

options.text: It picks words that sound likely, not ones it has checked are true
Its temperature was set too low
Its context window was too small
It's lying on purpose, to sound clever

cards.explanation: A title, an author and a summary all **sound** likely, so the model writes them, without checking they're true: a hallucination. A low temperature makes it more predictable, not more inventive, and a context window limits how much of the chat it can see, not whether it checks facts.

cards.prompt: Put the steps a chatbot repeats for every token in order.

items.label: Read all the text so far
Give each possible next token a chance
Add it to the end of the text

cards.explanation: Read, give each token a chance, pick one, add it, and repeat.

cards.prompt: A chatbot gives you a date for your history homework.

steps.text: It says a famous ship sank in 1915, and gives a website as its source. What do you do?

choices.text: Use it: it gave a source
choices.consequence: Chatbots can invent sources too. A source only helps if you open it.

choices.text: Open the source and check it says 1915
choices.consequence: Right: a source you've checked is a source you can trust.

choices.text: Ask the chatbot again, to see if it says 1915 twice
choices.consequence: It can repeat the same mistake. Check outside the chatbot.

cards.explanation: Dates and sources are where hallucinations hide. **Open the source** (or find a trusted one) and check it really says what the chatbot claims.

cards.prompt: Match each word to what it means.

pairs.right: Predicts the next token from text
A word, or part of one
How much of the chat it can see

cards.explanation: A **language model** predicts the next **token** (a word or part of one); **temperature** sets how adventurous its picks are; a **hallucination** is a confident false answer; the **context window** is how much it can see at once.
